passage:
Sit down, Bhavna, and let me tell you about my worst client. I'm Minakshi, and twelve years ago I had a client who called himself "a friend of the family." He asked for a logo. Then version two. Then twelve. Every time I said the budget covered three, he sighed and said, "Just this once, and there's a big project coming."

The payment kept getting pushed. "Next week, next week." The big project never had a date. I worked nights and felt that I wasn't professional enough to say no.

It took a friend, a senior designer, to say, "This is not your failing. This is his pattern." After that I wrote a contract with milestones and an advance. When he refused it, I told him politely that I couldn't continue.

He was annoyed. But two better clients came within a month, and I slept properly again. Learn from my mistake, not from my patience.

qa.q: How many logo versions did the client eventually ask for?
qa.a: The client asked for twelve versions of the logo, though the budget covered three.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi keep working nights for that client?
qa.a: Minakshi felt not professional enough to say no and hoped the promised big project would come.

qa.q: What steps did Minakshi take to end the exploitation?
qa.a: Minakshi wrote a contract with milestones and an advance, and when the client refused it, politely ended the engagement.

qa.q: How might the client have seen Minakshi's polite refusal?
qa.a: The client was annoyed, probably because free revisions had become an expectation, and Minakshi's firmness meant that pattern ended.

grounding: Endless free revisions, delayed payments and vague promises signal exploitation; the elder Minakshi tells how contracts, milestones, advances and a polite ending fixed it.

passage:
"Ujjwal, just one more small change to the website. Then we're done."
"Himani, that's what you said about the last eleven changes."
"You're so talented, though. And once we grow, I'll give you all our future work."
"I appreciate that. But the second payment was due in July. It's September."
"Cash is tight. Next month, promise."
Ujjwal took a breath. His stomach had been in knots for weeks, and he'd blamed himself for not finishing. "Here's what I can do. I'll complete the agreed pages once the second payment comes in. Any new changes, I'll quote separately, with half in advance."
"That sounds very formal."
"It is. It protects both of us. I'll send a short contract with milestones today."
"And if I can't pay yet?"
"Then I'll pause the work until you can. No hard feelings. But I can't keep working unpaid."

qa.q: When was the second payment due?
How had Ujjwal been feeling before this conversation?
qa.a: He had felt anxious, with his stomach in knots for weeks, and had blamed himself for not finishing.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do to stop the exploitation?
qa.a: He tied the remaining work to the overdue payment, offered to quote new changes with half in advance, sent a contract with milestones, and was ready to pause politely.

qa.q: How might Himani see Ujjwal's new terms?
qa.a: Himani seems surprised and a little resistant, finding it formal, used to getting free changes with vague promises.

grounding: A client demands endless free revisions and delays payment with vague promises; the protagonist sees it is not his failing and sets contracts, milestones and advances.

passage:
I'm Ojas, and for eight months I edited videos for Nandini's travel channel. She was friendly, full of plans. "When we get sponsors, you'll be our head of production." Meanwhile, each video went through eight or nine rounds of changes, and my invoices got paid forty days late, then sixty.
I kept thinking I was doing something wrong. If I were faster, better, maybe she'd be happier.
Looking back, what changed it was a friend who looked at my messages and said, "This isn't you failing. This is someone taking advantage."
So I wrote to Nandini: from next month, two rounds of changes per video, anything more at a set rate, half the fee in advance, and a simple contract. I kept it polite.
She said I'd changed. I said my terms had. She stopped working with me a month later. I was sad, and also relieved. My new clients sign the contract without blinking.

qa.q: How late were Ojas's invoices getting paid?
What was Ojas feeling before the friend's comment?
qa.a: Ojas felt anxious and inadequate, believing the endless changes and late payments were a personal failing.

qa.q: What terms did Ojas set to end the exploitation?
qa.a: Two rounds of changes per video, a set rate for more, half the fee in advance, and a simple contract.

qa.q: How might Nandini have seen Ojas's new terms?
qa.a: Nandini seemed to feel put out, saying Ojas had changed, because the free extra work was ending.

grounding: A client exploits the protagonist with endless revisions, late payment and vague promises; the protagonist sees it is not a personal failing and sets clear terms.
